Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich's offense doesn't have a loud signature — nearly every schematic dial sits at or near league average, from play-action to tempo to screens. The one thing that stands out is restraint in the passing game, running slightly more than expected in a pass-heavy league. What the numbers do show clearly is results: +0.06 EPA/play ranks 14th, well above the league average of -0.01, which suggests execution is doing more work here than scheme novelty.

Andy Reid.blurb: Reid runs one of the more pass-heavy systems in the league — +6.0 over expected pass rate, fifth-highest among all callers — and layers in screens (10%, well above the 7% norm) and RPOs (4%, fourth-highest in the league) to keep defenses from teeing off on that tendency. Pre-snap motion sits meaningfully above average at 48%. The scheme creativity score of 58 is genuinely elevated, though the honest caveat here is that scheme value reads as middling (-0.017, indicative only), and with this quarterback, it's nearly impossible to know how much of the production belongs to the system versus the player running it.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's offense sits near the top of the league in scheme value — +0.101 against a league average of -0.013, third among 76 coaches — built around two things that genuinely stand out: play-action at 25% (league average is 18%) and a fast pace at 82 plays per game (league average 75). Everything else is pretty conventional — motion, screens, pass tendency, and creativity all land right around the norm. The results back the approach: +0.09 EPA/play, tenth in the league.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer's Dallas offense is almost entirely conventional — motion, play-action, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league average, and at 44/100 the scheme rates a little below the midpoint on structural variety. The one thing worth noting is tempo: 81 plays per game against a league norm of 75, which is a real operational choice, not a rounding error. Results came in slightly above average at +0.04 EPA/play, but this system ran with effectively one quarterback the whole window, so whether that reflects the scheme or the QB is genuinely impossible to say.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Petzing runs one of the more conventional systems in the league — creativity scores at 41 against a 50 average, and most of his other tendencies sit right at or near league norms. What separates him from a pure vanilla label is a slightly elevated play-action rate (22% vs. 18% average) and results that are modestly above average at +0.04 EPA/play. The scheme value lands in the middle of the pack at #19, which is about right: a competent, execution-first offense that doesn't ask the system to do the heavy lifting.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's offense leans on play-action (22%, against a league norm of 18%) and touches RPOs at a slightly elevated rate, but beyond those two wrinkles this is a fairly conventional operation — motion, tempo, screen rate, and overall creativity all sit at or near league average. The results match the profile: -0.02 EPA/play, essentially league average and nothing that stands out in either direction.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's offense is almost entirely average by the numbers — creativity, pass tendency, play-action, and screens all sit right at league norm — with two modest exceptions: pre-snap motion runs at 48%, meaningfully above the 40% league average, and tempo pushes to 80 plays per game versus a 75-play norm. The results land slightly below average at -0.03 EPA/play, which isn't alarming but isn't a selling point either. A middle-of-the-pack system producing middle-of-the-pack outcomes.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell's offense is largely conventional — tempo, motion, pass tendency, and creativity all sit right at league average — with one genuine outlier: he leans on play-action at a 23% rate, well above the 18% league norm. The problem is that the results haven't backed it up, with EPA/play at -0.06 against a league average of -0.01, and scheme value at -0.042, both below average. The play-action emphasis is a real identity; what it's produced in Minnesota so far is a harder sell.

Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Shanahan's system ranks first in scheme value over this stretch — meaning even after adjusting for quarterback quality and opponent, the structure itself is generating real offensive edge. The one thing that stands out stylistically is pre-snap motion: 59% of dropbacks, well above the 40% league norm, which is the mechanism behind a lot of what his offense creates. Everything else — play-action, tempo, pass tendency, screens — sits right at league average, which is the honest read: this isn't an exotic system, it's a precise one that happens to produce elite results.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system grades out near the top of the league in scheme value, though the honest caveat is that the number is hard to fully separate from the quarterback — treat it as indicative of a strong system, not a certified rank. What's notable is how unremarkable the stylistic profile looks: creativity, motion, play-action, tempo, and screens all sit right at or near league average, with a slight lean toward the run. The output has been quietly excellent regardless, which is its own kind of statement.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy's Giants offense sits close to league average on most structural dimensions — creativity, motion, tempo, and play-action all land in the middle of the pack — but two things stand out: he passes at a notably higher rate than expected given game script, and his RPO usage at 4% is among the highest in the league against a 2% norm. Results have been marginally positive at +0.03 EPA/play, though with effectively one quarterback running this system throughout, it's impossible to say how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the player running it.

Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's Arizona offense leans heavily on pre-snap motion — 52% of dropbacks, well above the ~40% league norm — while running almost no RPOs (effectively zero against a 2% average) and sitting squarely at league average on tempo, screens, and play-action. The system produced above-average EPA results, but it ran with one quarterback throughout, so there's no clean way to separate what LaFleur built from what the quarterback provided — the style is identifiable, the value isn't.

Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the more structurally distinctive offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 59% of dropbacks (league norm is around 40%, top-4 in the NFL) and a screen rate of 10% against a 7% average signal a system built on manufactured leverage before and after the snap. The wrinkle is that it comes with a run-heavy lean (5.1 percentage points below expected pass rate) and scheme value sitting at -0.045 against a league average of -0.013, meaning the complexity isn't translating to a systemic edge — at least not yet with this roster.

Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's offense runs on pre-snap motion (53% of dropbacks, well above the ~40% league norm) and play-action (23% vs. 18% average) — two levers he pulls harder than most. The creativity score sits right at the middle of the pack, so this isn't an exotic system; it's a conventional structure executed with specific, deliberate emphases. Scheme value grades out positively at +0.061, though with only moderate reliability given his quarterback situation, treat that as directionally encouraging rather than definitive.

Sean Payton.blurb: Payton's Denver offense lands in an interesting middle ground: creativity scores notably high at 58/100 against a 50/100 league average, driven largely by a screen rate (10%) and RPO usage (3%) that both run well above norm, while pre-snap motion sits below average at 34% versus the league's 40%. Everything else — pass tendency, play-action, tempo — is essentially ordinary. Scheme value comes in at +0.023 against a league average of -0.013, a modest positive, though results (-0.02 EPA/play) have been roughly league-average, suggesting the system's upside hasn't fully materialized yet.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Shane Steichen's system ranks 7th in QB- and opponent-adjusted scheme value at +0.051, a meaningful gap above the league average of -0.013, which says the design itself is generating returns beyond personnel. The stylistic profile is mostly conventional — motion, tempo, screen rate, and pass tendency all sit near league norms — with modest upticks in play-action (22% vs. 18% average) and RPOs (3% vs. 2%). Results so far are roughly average at -0.02 EPA/play, so the scheme value hasn't fully shown up in outputs yet.

Todd Monken.blurb: Todd Monken's Cleveland offense sits almost perfectly at league average across every measurable dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, RPOs, screens, pass tendency, all of it within rounding distance of the norm. What stands out is the scheme value sitting indicatively in the top tier at +0.051 against a league average of -0.013, though with only moderate reliability it's hard to fully disentangle from the quarterback. The honest read: this is a clean, conventional system that has produced above-average results, and the style itself gives you no obvious reason why.

Wes Phillips.blurb: Phillips runs a mostly conventional offense — tempo, motion, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league average, and his creativity score lands exactly at the median. The one real differentiator is play-action, which he deploys on 23% of dropbacks against an 18% league norm, a genuine lean. The results haven't backed it up, though: -0.06 EPA/play ranks 54th, a meaningful gap below the league average of -0.01.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Zac Taylor runs one of the most pass-heavy systems in the league — +8.0 over expected pass rate, second among 76 play-callers — while keeping almost everything else at or near league average: motion at 40%, tempo at 77 plays per game, play-action slightly below norm at 15%. The creativity score (40/100, 68th) confirms it: this isn't a scheme built on disguise or pre-snap complexity, it's built on volume and execution in the passing game. That approach grades out as genuinely above-average system value (+0.034 against a league mean of -0.013, 11th overall), which means the aggression through the air isn't just a tendency — it's producing real schematic worth.

Bobby Slowik.blurb: Slowik runs one of the more exotic systems in the league — creativity scores in the top 10, with pre-snap motion on 47% of dropbacks above the 40% norm — but the outputs haven't matched the design. His offense ranks 55th in EPA/play at -0.06 against a league average of -0.01, and scheme value sits at -0.081 versus -0.013 average, though with only moderate reliability that number is indicative rather than definitive. The clearest through-line is a genuine run lean: pass rate nearly four points below expectation, ranking 64th. Creative by structure, conservative by tendency, and so far underwater on results.

Brad Idzik.blurb: Idzik's system is about as conventional as it gets on paper — creativity, tempo, play-action, RPOs, and screens all sit right at or near league average. The one thing that stands out is his pre-snap motion rate: 31%, noticeably below the ~40% league norm, meaning he's running a relatively static pre-snap offense. His scheme value comes in at +0.025 against a league average of -0.013, which is a decent number, though with only moderate reliability it's hard to fully disentangle from the quarterback. Results land right around average at +0.01 EPA/play — a functional system, not a distinctive one.

Dan Pitcher.blurb: Pitcher's system is about as conventional as it gets structurally — motion, tempo, RPOs, and screens all sit right at league average — but the defining characteristic is an aggressive pass-lean that ranks third in the league at +7.8 over expected, against a norm of -0.8. That's not situational; that's a philosophy. Play-action is actually below average at 14%, so this isn't a deception-based passing game — it's just a commitment to throwing it. The offense has produced a positive EPA/play, which is more than most can say.

Frank Smith.blurb: Frank Smith's offense is defined by two things above almost everyone else in the league: pre-snap motion on 70% of dropbacks (league average is 40%, and no one ranks higher) and a screen rate of 13% against a 7% norm, second in the league. Layer in play-action at 25% — well above the 18% average — and you have a system built on manufacturing stress before and after the snap. Pass tendency and tempo are ordinary, and the results land right around league average, so the pre-snap complexity isn't translating into a clear EPA edge yet.

Joe Brady.blurb: Brady's system sits near the top of the creativity rankings — 73/100 against a league average of 50 — and pre-snap motion at 50% of dropbacks (above the ~40% norm) is a big part of why defenses have trouble reading it pre-snap. Everything else is essentially average: play-action, RPO, screen rate, and tempo all land right at league norms, which means the complexity is coming from alignment and motion, not volume or pace. The +0.18 EPA/play is elite, though how much of that is scheme versus quarterback is genuinely hard to disentangle — the +0.025 scheme value is indicative of a real edge, but only moderately reliable given the context.

Joe Lombardi.blurb: Lombardi's Denver offense leans on a few tools more heavily than most — play-action at 24% (league avg 18%), screens at 12% (more than double the 7% norm), and RPOs at 4% against a 2% average — which earns the scheme a legitimately high creativity score without being exotic for its own sake. Pre-snap motion and pass tendency both sit close to league average, so this isn't a system built on disguise or aggression; it's built on specific constraint-stressing concepts used at real volume. The results were dead even at +0.00 EPA/play, which is fine but not an endorsement.

Klint Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's Las Vegas offense is about as close to league-average as a system gets — pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and screens all land right at the norm. The one genuine deviation is pre-snap motion, which he uses on 48% of dropbacks against a ~40% league average, suggesting he's leaning on that tool to manufacture advantage where the rest of the scheme is deliberately conventional. Scheme value sits at +0.019 against a league average of -0.013, a modest positive, and EPA/play is effectively zero — both middle-of-the-pack reads that say this is a functional, unspectacular operation.

Liam Coen.blurb: Coen's system doesn't announce itself with any particular stylistic signature — motion, tempo, play-action, and RPO usage all sit right at league average — but the results are hard to argue with: +0.10 EPA/play ranks fifth league-wide, and his QB-adjusted scheme value of +0.098 ranks fourth among 76 coaches, meaning the system itself is generating real value beyond whoever is running it. The honest read is that this is a clean, conventional offense that earns its production through execution and design quality, not exotic looks.

Nathaniel Hackett.blurb: Hackett's Arizona tenure was about as conventional as it gets — motion at 28% against a 40% league norm, play-action and RPOs both sitting below average, screens exactly at the mean. The one thing that stands out is how little creativity the system generated (36/100, near the bottom of the league), though minimalism isn't inherently a problem. The results, though, were: -0.10 EPA/play ranked 63rd, and a QB-adjusted scheme value of -0.066 against a league average of -0.013, meaning the system itself wasn't adding much regardless of personnel.

Press Taylor.blurb: Press Taylor's system is about as close to league-average as an offense can be across the board — motion at 31% against a 40% norm is the one real deviation, and it runs notably still by modern standards. The indicative scheme value of +0.035 looks solid, but reliability is only moderate given how intertwined the results are with his quarterback situation, so that number is a signal, not a verdict. Results landed right around the middle at -0.02 EPA/play.

Zac Robinson.blurb: Robinson runs one of the more run-heavy systems in the league — nearly 6 fewer pass attempts over expected per game than the norm — and pairs that with a low-creativity approach (40/100 against a league average of 50) that leans on structure over variety. Pre-snap motion at 48% is a genuine wrinkle, sitting above the league average of 40%, but most other markers sit right at the mean. The results so far are slightly below average at -0.04 EPA/play, and the scheme value of -0.068 against a league average of -0.013 suggests the system itself isn't adding much on top of personnel.

Alex Van Pelt.blurb: Van Pelt ran the fastest offense in the league at 86 plays per game — well above the 75-game average — and that's essentially the one distinguishing feature of his system. Everything else sits right at the norm: motion (39% vs. 40% avg), play-action (20% vs. 18%), screen rate (9% vs. 7%). The results were poor at -0.11 EPA/play, and the QB-adjusted scheme value of -0.057 ranked 31st — meaning the system itself wasn't adding much beyond volume.

Arthur Smith.blurb: Arthur Smith runs a run-heavy, play-action-forward system — pass rate is well below the league norm, but he compensates with play-action at 23% (against an 18% average) and screens at 10% (against 7%), giving the passing game structure without asking it to carry the offense. Everything else — motion, tempo, RPOs — sits right at league average. The results land exactly at the league median, which is honest: this is a functional, coherent system that doesn't ask more than it delivers.

Declan Doyle.blurb: Doyle's offense scores a 63 on the creativity index — well above the 50 league average — yet the surface-level mechanics are almost entirely ordinary: motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sit right at league norms. The exoticness lives somewhere less visible, in structure and sequencing rather than raw pre-snap volume. Results are strong at +0.10 EPA/play, and the scheme value reads as a top-five system, though that number carries only moderate reliability given the quarterback situation — treat it as a real signal, not a confirmed ranking.

Doug Nussmeier.blurb: Nussmeier runs a straightforward offense — conventional tempo, average motion and pass rate, almost no RPOs — and the one dimension that stands out is what's missing: play-action at 13% and screens at 3% are both well below league norms of 18% and 7%. That's a scheme that doesn't lean on constraint plays, which is a legitimate philosophy, though the -0.07 EPA/play suggests it hasn't fully paid off yet. Worth noting he's currently in an OC role without play-calling duties.

Eric Bieniemy.blurb: Bieniemy's Kansas City offense was among the most pass-heavy in the league — +7.0 over expected, fourth in the window — but it ran deliberately, with pre-snap motion at 28% (well below the ~40% norm) and a slower pace than most. The honest caveat here is that the system's actual worth can't be separated from Patrick Mahomes, so what reads as offensive creativity (57/100, modestly above average) may be more quarterback than coordinator. Results were positive but unremarkable at +0.03 EPA/play, which tracks: this was a competent operation built around an exceptional talent, and the scheme was a vehicle more than a driver.

Grant Udinski.blurb: Udinski's Jacksonville offense doesn't stand out for anything exotic — creativity, motion, play-action, and screens all sit right around league average — but it passes more than almost anyone would expect given the situation, running +2.8 over expected pass rate against a league norm of -0.8. The pace is deliberately slow at 72 plays per game, one of the lower marks in the league. What makes it work is the production: +0.09 EPA/play, eighth-best among 76 play-callers, which suggests the choices, conventional as they look, are consistently the right ones.

Greg Roman.blurb: Roman's system in Los Angeles is defined most clearly by its play-action volume — 27% of dropbacks, second in the league against an 18% norm — paired with pre-snap motion on 52% of plays, well above the 40% average. Everything else sits close to league typical: creativity, tempo, RPO and screen usage are all middle of the pack. The scheme-value number is positive and above average, but reliability is only moderate given the quarterback context, so treat it as a directional read rather than a firm verdict.

Josh McDaniels.blurb: McDaniels ran a notably stripped-down offense in New England — almost no screens (4% against a 7% league norm), virtually no RPOs (1% vs. 2%), and below-average motion and play-action across the board. By structure, it's about as conventional as it gets. The results were strong (+0.10 EPA/play, sixth in the sample), but this scheme ran almost entirely through one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate what the system produced from what the QB produced.

Ken Dorsey.blurb: Dorsey runs one of the fastest offenses in the league — 85 plays per game against a 75-play norm, which puts him second overall — and pairs that pace with a pass tendency that runs meaningfully above average. Everything else sits right at the league mean: motion, play-action, RPOs, screens, creativity. The results have been below average at -0.04 EPA/play, and the scheme value lands similarly, which makes the volume a reasonable question: pushing the pace this aggressively while the underlying numbers trail isn't obviously a winning formula.

Klay Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak runs a pass-heavy offense — +3.4 over expected, well above the league's -0.8 baseline — with virtually no RPOs (0%, compared to a 2% norm) and below-average tempo at 68 plays per game. The structure is deliberate and conventional in most respects, but it produced +0.15 EPA/play, third-best in the league. The results say the scheme doesn't need to be exotic to work.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams runs one of the most conventional offensive schemes in the league — nearly every structural lever sits exactly at league average, and screens are the one notable outlier, coming in at 4% against a 7% norm. What stands out isn't the design, it's the output: +0.09 EPA/play ranks 9th across all 76 play-callers, well above the league average of -0.01. Sometimes the most honest read is that the execution is doing the heavy lifting.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's Washington offense is built around pre-snap manipulation — play-action on 26% of dropbacks (league average is 18%, top-3 leaguewide) and RPOs on 4% (double the norm, also top-3), giving defenses a lot to account to before the ball is snapped. The system rates as genuinely exotic by structure, scoring 64/100 on creativity against a league average of 50. Scheme value comes in at +0.048 (indicative, not precise — the sample is tied enough to one quarterback that clean separation is difficult), and results have been strong at +0.07 EPA/play, though the same caveat applies.

Luke Getsy.blurb: Getsy runs a genuinely up-tempo operation — 83 plays per game ranks eighth across the sample, and he pairs that pace with pre-snap motion on 51% of dropbacks, well above the 40% league norm. The rest of the scheme is ordinary: play-action, RPOs, screens, and pass tendency all sit near league average. The results, though, are hard to overlook: -0.10 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, ranking 64th of 76, and a scheme value of -0.052 against an average of -0.013 — suggesting the system itself isn't generating value, not just the personnel.

Mike Kafka.blurb: Kafka's system is almost entirely average across the board — motion, play-action, screens, RPO usage, and creativity all sit right at league norms — with one genuine outlier: he pushes tempo hard, running 83 plays per game against a league average of 75, good for 9th overall. The problem is that pace hasn't produced anything; the Giants ranked 72nd of 76 in EPA/play at -0.14, and even after adjusting for quarterback and opponent, the scheme itself graded out below average. More snaps, worse results.

Mike McCarthy.blurb: McCarthy's Pittsburgh offense passes more than almost anyone — +3.6 over expected, ninth-highest in the league — but does so without the play-action that typically makes passing attacks work, running it on just 12% of dropbacks against an 18% league norm. Everything else sits at or near average: tempo, motion, screens, RPO usage. The results have been poor (-0.09 EPA/play, 62nd of 76), and the scheme value lands below average too, so the style isn't hiding anything the numbers aren't already saying.

Nick Caley.blurb: Nick Caley's Houston offense is almost entirely average by the numbers — motion, tempo, play-action, and pass tendency all sit right at or within a hair of league norm. The one real outlier is screens, where he runs them at roughly half the league rate (3% vs. 7%), suggesting a deliberate preference for structured routes over short-area releases. Results land just above league average at +0.01 EPA/play, though with moderate reliability on scheme value, how much of that belongs to the system versus the quarterback remains genuinely unclear.

Nick Holz.blurb: Holz runs a conventional system — motion, play-action, tempo, and personnel usage all sit right around league norms — with one real outlier: he calls pass plays at a significantly lower rate than almost anyone in the league, running 6.5 percentage points below expectation, third-lowest among the 76 coaches tracked. The scheme value lands below average at -0.110, and the results back that up with an EPA/play of -0.14, both ranking near the bottom of the league. The run-heavy philosophy isn't inherently wrong, but right now the execution isn't making the case for it.

Shane Waldron.blurb: Waldron's system is mostly conventional — creativity, motion, play-action, and tempo all sit near league average — but one thing stands out: screens on 12% of dropbacks, well above the 7% league norm and a top-4 rate in the sample. Beyond that signature, the results have been modest, with scheme value at -0.028 against a league average of -0.013, and overall EPA/play slightly below average, suggesting the screen-heavy approach hasn't moved the needle enough on its own.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Giants offense runs fast — 82 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and leans heavily on play-action (24% vs. 18% average) and screens (10% vs. 7%), which together suggest a system built around manufacturing easy throws rather than beating defenses with complexity. He runs the ball more than almost anyone, sitting 4.3 points below expected pass rate, though the results so far are middling at -0.02 EPA/play. Scheme value comes in at -0.009, slightly better than the league average of -0.013 — functional, not impressive.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs one of the more run-heavy systems in the league — passing 6.8 percentage points below expected, with essentially no RPO usage against a 2% league norm — and does it at a slow pace (70 plays per game versus the 75-play average). The rest of the scheme is unremarkable: motion, play-action, and screen rates all sit near league average. What's harder to ignore is that the results haven't followed: -0.12 EPA/play ranks 68th of 76, and QB-adjusted scheme value lands below average at -0.172, suggesting the system itself isn't generating much.

Andrew Janocko.blurb: Janocko runs one of the more stripped-down offenses in the league — almost no play-action (8% against an 18% norm), minimal motion (22% vs. 40%), essentially zero RPOs, and a slow pace that ranks near the bottom. The creativity score reflects all of that. What keeps it from being a knock is the EPA: +0.02 per play, above league average, suggests the simplicity is at least executing.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio runs a stripped-down passing offense — almost no play-action (7% against an 18% league norm), virtually no motion (18% vs. 40%), and zero RPOs — but leans heavily pass despite all of it, sitting sixth in pass rate over expected at +5.5. The result is an offense that telegraphs its intentions and generated below-average EPA at -0.08 per play. Straightforward by design, but the execution didn't hold up the bet.

Brian Daboll.blurb: Daboll's Tennessee offense sits at the extreme low end of nearly every structural measure — 17% pre-snap motion against a 40% league norm, play-action at 8% versus 18%, screens at 2% versus 7%, and a pace of just 53 plays per game, last in the league. The results have been poor at -0.15 EPA/play, though because the system has run with effectively one quarterback, there's no clean way to separate the scheme's contribution from the QB's. What's clear is the style: slow, run-heavy, and stripped down — whether that's a choice or a constraint is the open question.

Brian Fleury.blurb: Fleury runs one of the more deliberately stripped-down offenses in the league — below average in nearly every wrinkle category, from play-action at 12% (league avg 18%) to pre-snap motion at 25% (league avg 40%), with tempo sitting at just 62 plays per game against a league norm of 75. The system also leans run more than almost anyone, with pass rate nearly five points below expectation. Whether that minimalism is working is genuinely hard to say: this scheme has run with effectively one quarterback, so the -0.08 EPA/play can't be cleanly separated from the QB's own contribution.

Chip Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Las Vegas offense had two real signatures: pre-snap motion on 56% of dropbacks (league norm is around 40%) and play-action on 25% of snaps (league avg 18%), both well above average and consistent with his long-standing preference for pre-snap manipulation. Everything else — tempo, RPO usage, screen rate, pass tendency — sat right at league average. The scheme-value number is indicative at best given the QB situation, but the results were unambiguous: dead last in EPA/play at -0.21 against a league average of -0.01.

Dave Canales.blurb: Dave Canales runs a broadly conventional offense — motion, screens, pass tendency, and creativity all sit right around league average — with two real distinguishing marks: an RPO rate of 4%, well above the ~2% norm, and a pace that trends toward the faster end at 81 plays per game. Play-action at 22% is a modest uptick from the 18% average. The EPA sits at -0.02, essentially league average, but this system ran with one quarterback throughout, so how much of that reflects the scheme versus the QB is genuinely hard to separate.

David Blough.blurb: Blough's offense is defined more by what it doesn't do than what it does: play-action at 8% against an 18% league norm, pre-snap motion at 20% against 40%, screens near zero, RPOs completely absent. It's a stripped-down system that asks the quarterback to process and throw with minimal pre-snap manipulation. Results land right at league average (-0.01 EPA/play), and scheme value is marginally above average but only moderately reliable given the limited sample — so the honest read is that this is an unadorned system that hasn't hurt, but hasn't clearly added much either.

Davis Webb.blurb: Webb's Denver offense was defined more by what it didn't do than what it did — play-action at 9% against a league average of 18%, pre-snap motion at 23% against 40%, screens at 4% against 7%, and a tempo of 57 plays per game that ranked 75th of 76. That's a slow, stripped-down operation across the board, not a philosophical minimalism so much as a constrained one, and the -0.08 EPA/play reflects it.

Frank Reich.blurb: Reich's Jets offense in 2023 was about as stripped-down as it gets: pre-snap motion on just 14% of dropbacks (league average is around 40%), play-action on 8% (league average 18%), and one of the slowest tempos in the league at 58 plays per game. Nearly every schematic dial was turned down, not just one. The results landed near league average at -0.03 EPA/play, but this system ran essentially on one quarterback, so there's no reliable way to separate Reich's effect from his QB's — the style is clear, the value isn't.

John Morton.blurb: Morton runs one of the league's more structurally distinctive offenses even if its true value can't be separated from his quarterback: play-action on 26% of dropbacks (league average is 18%, fourth in the league) and pre-snap motion on 59% (third, against a ~40% norm) are the load-bearing pieces, layered over a screen game that runs well above average at 10%. The scheme is otherwise conventional — low creativity rating, below-average pass tendency, almost no RPOs — so the results (+0.08 EPA/play, 11th) look like a system that wins through a few well-developed tools run at high tempo, not breadth.

Josh Grizzard.blurb: Grizzard's system has three genuine outliers: pre-snap motion on 58% of dropbacks (league average is around 40%), screens at 10% (league average 7%), and a tempo that pushes 84 plays per game against a league average of 75. Everything else — play-action, RPO usage, pass tendency, creativity — sits right at the middle of the league.
